title: Barren Plateaus
summary: Gradients of random deep circuits vanish exponentially with the number of qubits.
objectives: Estimate how big a gradient is at a random starting point by sampling it over random angles
Say how the size of the gradient and the number of shots needed to see it scale with the number of qubits
Say why a cost on all qubits is harder to train than one on a few qubits
mission: The gradients of random circuits shrink as the circuit grows. The ansatz has n layers on n qubits, each layer an R_Y(θ) on every qubit followed by a chain of CZ gates between neighbours, and the cost is the expectation of Z on all qubits at once. Complete gradient_variance(n, layers, samples) so that it returns the variance of ∂C/∂θ for the first angle (layer 0, qubit 0) over random angles in [0, 2π), and store the results for 2 to 6 qubits, 100 samples each, in variances. The variance for 6 qubits must be below 0.3 times the variance for 2 qubits.

prediction.question: For the product ansatz of the text (one R_Y per qubit, cost Z on all qubits), the gradient variance is 2⁻ⁿ. With n = 10, about how many shots per evaluation does it take before shot noise stops hiding a typical gradient?
options: About a thousand: the typical gradient is 2⁻⁵ and the shot error is 1/√N
About a million, since the variance is 2⁻¹⁰ and the shots must be its inverse squared
prediction.explanation: A typical gradient is the standard deviation, 2^(−10/2) = 2⁻⁵ = 1/32. The statistical error of an evaluation with N shots is about 1/√N, so it drops below 1/32 for N around 32² = 1,024 = 2¹⁰. Taking the variance 2⁻¹⁰ as the size of the gradient would give a factor 2²⁰, about a million, which overstates the cost.

hints: The gradient of one parameter needs the circuit at θ + π/2 and θ − π/2. How would you shift only the first angle, layer 0 and qubit 0?

Draw theta = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, (layers, n)) and make two copies, with π/2 added to entry [0][0] of one and subtracted from the other. The gradient is half the difference of the two circuit values. Inside the QNode, apply RY then the CZ chain for each layer and return the product of Z on every qubit.
Collect the gradients of the 100 samples in a list and return float(np.var(gradients)). Then build variances with one call per width, using layers = n.

challenge.mission: The mission's cost asks about all n qubits at once, and its gradient disappears as n grows. Keep the same ansatz at a fixed depth of 2 layers and ask a smaller question instead. Write local_variance(n, layers, samples), which works like gradient_variance but with the cost Z on qubit 0 alone. Then store in n_values the widths 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, and in local_vars and global_vars the variances of the local and of the global cost for those widths, with 2 layers and 100 samples each. The validator simulates both costs itself and compares every stored value with its own, calls local_variance on a circuit of its own, and requires the local variance at 10 qubits to be at least 0.4 times the one at 2 qubits while the global one is below 0.05 times.
hints: Only one line of the mission's circuit decides which cost you are measuring. What does qml.expval have to return for a cost on qubit 0 alone?
Copy gradient_variance under a new name and change the returned expectation to qml.PauliZ(0). Build n_values, then one list per cost with the same layers = 2 in both.

With a single layer the cost Z on qubit 0 equals cos θ for the first angle, so its gradient is −sin θ and its variance is 1/2 at any width. The validator uses that value to tell the local cost from the global one.
